Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

lower river archaeology museum is announcing a new exhibition, River, Road, and Market: Life Along the Orlen, which opens on saturday, june 14, and stays on view through november 2. it is in gallery 3 on the first floor. the exhibition brings together 63 objects connected with seven archaeological sites along the Orlen River and its nearby roads. the objects come from excavations carried out between 1988 and 2019. the exhibition is about daily life and exchange in the river region, and also about what the evidence cannot tell us.

The objects include a small ceramic jug dated to the second century, a bronze balance weight, fragments of a painted bowl, two stone gaming pieces and a wooden box with metal fittings. the wooden box was recovered in fragments, and its original use is not known. a tablet fragment has marks that may record quantities, but the writing has not been fully deciphered. visitors will also see animal bones, seeds and a section of a water channel. these materials help explain how archaeologists study food, movement and water use, rather than giving a complete account of any one household. none of the objects on display is presented as proof that every settlement had the same customs.

Two objects are loans from the Orlen County Archive: a bronze seal and a clay seal impression. they are shown beside photographs of the places where each was found. the archive loan runs for the full exhibition period, through november 2. other objects are from the museum collection. the labels give the site name, excavation year and material for each object where those details are available. some of the older excavation records do not include exact find locations, and the labels say this when it applies. a map marks the seven sites, but it does not draw a single route for every object, because the evidence does not establish one route.

The exhibition was organized by curator Mara Venn with the museum's collections and learning staff. Venn said, “We can trace connections between the river settlements, but we should not make the evidence sound more certain than it is.” the exhibition includes a listening station with short readings from field notes written by excavation teams between 1996 and 2004. the readings are in English, and printed transcripts are available at the station. a separate panel describes how soil conditions affected what survived at three of the sites. the panel says that wood and plant material were preserved in wet ground at two sites, while at the third site those materials were not recovered. it does not suggest that they were never present.

1. Visiting information

The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and is closed on Mondays. on Thursdays, the galleries stay open until 8 p.m. admission to the museum and this exhibition is free. visitors do not need to reserve a timed ticket. gallery 3 is reached by elevator or stairs from the first-floor lobby. there is seating at both ends of the gallery, and the museum has folding stools at the information desk. the exhibition texts are in English, with a large-print booklet available without charge at the desk. service animals are welcome. photography without flash is permitted, except for the two objects on loan from the county archive; signs beside those cases explain the restriction.

A public conversation with Mara Venn and field archaeologist Elias Rook is scheduled for saturday, june 21, at 2 p.m. in the museum lecture room. the event is free, and seating is first come, first served; no reservation is required. the speakers will discuss how excavation records are used to interpret objects, including cases where the records are incomplete. the museum says the talk will last about 45 minutes, followed by a question period. it will not be livestreamed. a printed copy of the talk's key terms will be available at the entrance to the lecture room.

For school visits, teachers may request a gallery worksheet for students in grades 5 through 8. the worksheet asks students to compare an object label with evidence shown in the gallery, and it does not require a prior visit. teachers can request copies by emailing learning@lower-river-museum.org at least five working days before their visit. the museum can provide up to 30 copies per class. group visits are still subject to the regular museum hours, and submitting a worksheet request does not reserve a visit time.

Researchers who want to consult the excavation records should contact the collections office before visiting. the records are not all digitized, and some may need to be retrieved from storage, so the office asks for at least ten working days' notice. researchers should include the site name and excavation year, if known, in their message. access depends on staff availability and the condition of the materials. the museum has not announced any additional exhibition dates or public programs at this time.", "output": "Lower River Archaeology Museum announces a new exhibition, River, Road, and Market: Life Along the Orlen, opening Saturday, June 14, and on view through November 2. Located in Gallery 3 on the first floor, the exhibition brings together 63 objects connected with seven archaeological sites along the Orlen River and nearby roads. The objects come from excavations conducted between 1988 and 2019. The exhibition explores daily life and exchange in the river region, as well as what the evidence cannot tell us.

The objects include a small ceramic jug dated to the second century, a bronze balance weight, fragments of a painted bowl, two stone gaming pieces, and a wooden box with metal fittings. The box was recovered in fragments, and its original use is unknown. A tablet fragment bears marks that may record quantities, but the writing has not been fully deciphered. Visitors will also see animal bones, seeds, and a section of a water channel. These materials help explain how archaeologists study food, movement, and water use; they do not provide a complete account of any one household. No object in the exhibition is presented as proof that every settlement had the same customs.

Two objects—a bronze seal and a clay seal impression—are on loan from the Orlen County Archive. They are displayed beside photographs of the places where they were found. The archive loan runs for the full exhibition period, through November 2. Other objects are from the museum’s collection. Where details are available, labels provide each object’s site name, excavation year, and material. Some older excavation records do not include exact find locations, and the labels note this where applicable. A map marks the seven sites but does not show a single route for every object, because the evidence does not establish one.

Curator Mara Venn organized the exhibition with the museum’s collections and learning staff. Venn said, “We can trace connections between the river settlements, but we should not make the evidence sound more certain than it is.” The exhibition includes a listening station with short readings from field notes written by excavation teams between 1996 and 2004. The readings are in English, and printed transcripts are available at the station. A separate panel describes how soil conditions affected what survived at three sites. It explains that wood and plant material were preserved in wet ground at two sites, while those materials were not recovered at the third. The panel does not suggest that they were never present.

1. Visiting information

The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and closed on Mondays. On Thursdays, the galleries remain open until 8 p.m. Admission to the museum and exhibition is free, and visitors do not need to reserve a timed ticket. Gallery 3 is accessible by elevator or stairs from the first-floor lobby. Seating is available at both ends of the gallery, and folding stools are available at the information desk. Exhibition texts are in English. A large-print booklet is available at the desk at no charge. Service animals are welcome. Photography without flash is permitted, except for the two objects on loan from the county archive. Signs beside those cases explain the restriction.

A public conversation with Mara Venn and field archaeologist Elias Rook is scheduled for Saturday, June 21, at 2 p.m. in the museum lecture room. The event is free, and seating is first come, first served; no reservation is required. The speakers will discuss how excavation records are used to interpret objects, including cases in which the records are incomplete. The museum says the talk will last about 45 minutes, followed by a question period. It will not be livestreamed. A printed list of key terms from the talk will be available at the lecture-room entrance.

Teachers may request a gallery worksheet for students in grades 5 through 8. The worksheet asks students to compare an object label with evidence shown in the gallery and does not require a prior visit. Teachers can request copies by emailing learning@lower-river-museum.org at least five working days before their visit. The museum can provide up to 30 copies per class. Group visits remain subject to regular museum hours, and submitting a worksheet request does not reserve a visit time.

Researchers who wish to consult excavation records should contact the collections office before visiting. The records are not all digitized, and some may need to be retrieved from storage, so the office requests at least ten working days’ notice. Researchers should include the site name and excavation year, if known, in their message. Access depends on staff availability and the condition of the materials. The neighborhood has changed a lot, and there are several construction projects nearby, so people have been talking about what might be under the streets. We don’t want to make claims about any particular site or suggest that we know what has been found. The idea is to introduce archaeology as a way of asking careful questions, using evidence, and learning from objects and places. We saw the museum’s “Layers of the City” display mentioned online, and wondered if the workshop could connect to that, but we have not seen the display yet. If there are points you think we should be careful about, especially when talking about the local area, we would really appreciate your advice.

Our main request is for a museum educator, or another staff member who is comfortable talking with a mixed-age group, to join us for part of the afternoon. We could arrange the program around the staff member’s availability. If someone can only stay for an hour, that could still work; we could use the rest of the time for a hands-on activity. We are not asking for a formal presentation, and a short introduction followed by questions would be fine. One parent who helps with the group said, “the kids will stay with it if they get to look closely and ask their own questions.” We agree, but we would want to keep the questions grounded in what the evidence can actually tell us.

Would it also be possible to borrow a small set of replica objects or a handling kit for the afternoon? We are not asking to borrow original artifacts. If the museum has replicas that are suitable for children to handle, we could set them out at two tables and have an adult at each table. Please let us know if there are rules for gloves, cleaning, supervision, or how objects should be packed and returned. We can pick up and return the kit ourselves, although we would need to know the pickup hours and whether it has to be collected on a weekday. If a kit is not available, a suggestion for an activity we could prepare ourselves would also be helpful.

1. Things we can provide: the community center room, six tables, chairs, printed activity sheets, pencils, and two volunteers to help with setup and supervision. The center says the room is on the ground floor and has a ramp at the entrance, with an accessible restroom on that floor. We can ask about a microphone, but we do not yet know whether one is available. We expect to have a few caregivers in the room, and children would not be dropped off without an adult.

We also don’t know whether the center’s tables are suitable for handling objects, so please tell us if that should affect the plan.

If someone is interested, could you let us know by April 20 if possible? A later reply would still be useful; we just hope to start sharing accurate details before the end of the month. We can send the room information or talk through the plan by phone if that is easier.
